screens.title: Advanced Scriptable Objects & Editor Scripting
screens.subtitle: Authoring shared game data and building editor tools that speed up workflow

narration.text: In this lesson you’ll see why ScriptableObjects let teams treat data as first-class assets, and how Editor scripting turns repetitive setup into one-click tools. ScriptableObjects are persistent data containers that live in your project like textures or audio. They help you separate configuration from behavior, reduce duplicated memory, and make it easier for designers to create and tune content without touching code. Editor scripting complements this by letting programmers expose validation, batch operations, and tailored controls right in the Inspector or in custom windows. Together they enable workflows like a WeaponData asset that many GameObjects reference, a PlayerWeapon script that uses that data at runtime, and a custom inspector that gives designers useful buttons and color feedback. You’ll follow a mixed-format path: conceptual slides about data versus logic, a live coding demo creating WeaponData and PlayerWeapon, then a walk-through building a custom ItemData inspector and an Editor Window. By the end you’ll know where to keep each file, how to avoid common pitfalls, and how to design reusable tools that empower non-programmers. Ready to explore why this pattern matters in real projects and how to implement it practically?

screens.title: What is a ScriptableObject?
screens.subtitle: A persistent, shareable data asset — not a scene component

narration.text: A ScriptableObject is a Unity class designed to store data as an asset in your project. Unlike a MonoBehaviour, it is not attached to a GameObject in a scene; instead, you create instances as project assets that live in the Project window and persist across play sessions. This makes them ideal for configuration such as weapon stats, quest definitions, or game settings that many objects should reference. ScriptableObjects are primarily data containers. You can add methods to them, but the recommended pattern is to keep behavior in MonoBehaviours and keep ScriptableObjects as authorable, shareable data. A concrete example is a WeaponData asset that holds damage, range, fire rate, and references like a projectile prefab or an icon. Using assets reduces duplicated memory because many runtime objects can reference the same data object instead of each having their own copy. A common misconception is trying to store temporary runtime state inside ScriptableObjects; they are best used for persistent configuration. To check your understanding, think about where you'd store player preferences versus enemy templates, and why enemy templates belong in a ScriptableObject.

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: ScriptableObjects are persistent assets for shared configuration; use them for templates and settings, not ephemeral runtime state.

content.html:
Module 08 › Chapter 8.2 › What is a ScriptableObject?
Definition

ScriptableObject as a data asset

A persistent, shareable asset for configuration and content templates. Not tied to a scene object.

Best fit: item definitions, weapon templates, quest data.
Misuse to avoid: storing temporary runtime state.
Benefit: single source of truth reduces duplicated memory.
Key Takeaway

Treat ScriptableObjects as templates and configuration that multiple runtime objects can reference.

Example
// WeaponData: a ScriptableObject that stores weapon configuration
[CreateAssetMenu(fileName = "NewWeaponData", menuName = "Game Data/Weapon Data")]
public class WeaponData : ScriptableObject
{
    public string weaponName = "Default Weapon";
    public float damage = 10f;
    public float fireRate = 0.5f;
    public float range = 100f;
    public GameObject projectilePrefab;
    public Sprite icon;
}
Why this helps
  • Designers create many WeaponData assets without editing code.
  • MonoBehaviours reference the asset for behavior values at runtime.
  • Avoids copying the same variables onto many GameObjects.

screens.title: Creating ScriptableObject assets
screens.subtitle: Define the class, add CreateAssetMenu, and author assets in Project

narration.text: Creating a ScriptableObject asset follows a small, repeatable process. First, define a class that inherits from ScriptableObject and declare the public fields designers will edit. Second, add the CreateAssetMenu attribute so your asset type appears under Assets > Create, making it discoverable to non-programmers. Third, save the script and return to the Editor to create an instance; populate fields in the Inspector as you would with any asset. An example workflow is creating WeaponData with fields for damage, fire rate, range, and references like a projectile prefab or icon. Be deliberate about naming defaults and using enums for categories to make filtering easy. A common mistake is embedding runtime state or heavy logic in the asset; keep logic light and focused on data operations, reserving complex behaviors for the MonoBehaviour. Another pitfall is forgetting to mark assets dirty after programmatic edits in the Editor, which can prevent changes from persisting. The small checklist of steps, careful field selection, and attention to persistence will make your ScriptableObjects reliable, discoverable, and designer-friendly. Creating ScriptableObject assets means define scriptableobject fields, add createassetmenu, create and populate assets, and avoid storing ephemeral runtime state.. In practical terms, define the class, add createassetmenu, and author assets in project. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 08 › Chapter 8.2 › Create ScriptableObject
Steps

How to create an asset

  1. Declare class : ScriptableObject and public fields.
  2. Add [CreateAssetMenu] with fileName and menuName.
  3. Save script, open Unity, right-click Project > Create > your menu path.
  4. Fill fields in the Inspector and save the asset.
Common Mistake
Using ScriptableObjects for temporary runtime state or placing editor-only code in non-Editor folders can break builds.
Visual Example
[CreateAssetMenu(fileName = "NewWeaponData", menuName = "Game Data/Weapon Data")] 
public class WeaponData : ScriptableObject
{
    public string weaponName = "Default Weapon";
    public float damage = 10f;
    public float fireRate = 0.5f;
    public GameObject projectilePrefab;
}
Designer-friendly: appears in Assets > Create
Tip: use enums for categories to simplify editors

screens.title: Using ScriptableObjects at runtime
screens.subtitle: How a MonoBehaviour references and consumes data assets

narration.text: When you use a ScriptableObject in runtime code, the MonoBehaviour simply holds a reference to the asset and reads its fields when needed. The common pattern is to treat the asset as a configuration object. For example, a PlayerWeapon MonoBehaviour can have a public WeaponData field. In Update you check the input and timing, then use values from the WeaponData asset to control firing cadence and instantiation. This keeps the runtime script focused on behavior and the asset focused on data. One benefit is that designers can swap different WeaponData assets on a GameObject to change behavior without modifying code. A frequent misconception is expecting ScriptableObjects to manage scene-specific state; they are better suited for templates and shared constants. When interacting with prefabs via the asset, be sure to check for null references and only instantiate prefab references stored on the asset during runtime. The core takeaway is: ScriptableObjects provide centralized parameters; runtime scripts implement the behavior using those parameters. Using ScriptableObjects at runtime means monobehaviours reference scriptableobject assets for configuration; the asset supplies values while the component implements behavior.. In practical terms, how a monobehaviour references and consumes data assets. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Runtime usage
keyIdea.text: MonoBehaviours reference ScriptableObject assets for configuration; the asset supplies values while the component implements behavior.

content.html:
Module 08 › Chapter 8.2 › PlayerWeapon Example
Example Code
public class PlayerWeapon : MonoBehaviour
{
    public WeaponData currentWeapon; // Reference to a ScriptableObject asset
    private float nextFireTime;

    void Update()
    {
        if (currentWeapon == null) return;
        if (Input.GetButton("Fire1") && Time.time >= nextFireTime)
        {
            FireWeapon();
            nextFireTime = Time.time + 1f / currentWeapon.fireRate;
        }
    }

    void FireWeapon()
    {
        // Use data from the asset to control behavior
        if (currentWeapon.projectilePrefab != null)
        {
            Instantiate(currentWeapon.projectilePrefab, transform.position + transform.forward, transform.rotation);
        }
    }
}
Annotated Notes
  • Reference the asset via a public field so designers can assign it.
  • Read fields at runtime to drive timing, damage, and prefab instantiation.
  • Check for null asset or missing prefab to avoid runtime errors.
Analogy: asset is the blueprint; MonoBehaviour is the contractor that follows it.
Misconception: ScriptableObjects are not a replacement for component state like health or position during play.

screens.title: ScriptableObject vs MonoBehaviour
screens.subtitle: When to use assets versus components

narration.text: Deciding between storing data on a MonoBehaviour versus using a ScriptableObject depends on scope and intent. MonoBehaviours are tied to a specific GameObject and are ideal for scene-specific state and behavior, such as a character's current health, position, or temporary flags. ScriptableObjects live in the Project and are best for templates, configurations, and shared assets like enemy types or weapon definitions. A clear example: instead of giving every weapon instance a duplicate set of damage and rate variables on their MonoBehaviour, create WeaponData assets and have the MonoBehaviour reference them. This reduces memory duplication and centralizes tuning. Keep logic that depends on instance state in MonoBehaviours; use ScriptableObjects for stable parameters. A common mistake is trying to use ScriptableObjects for ephemeral, scene-only data. Conversely, putting large catalogs of shared configuration into ScriptableObjects dramatically improves designer workflows. To test this, ask whether the value changes per instance and per session; if not, it belongs in an asset. ScriptableObject vs MonoBehaviour means use scriptableobjects for shared, persistent templates; use monobehaviours for instance-specific, runtime state and logic.. In practical terms, when to use assets versus components. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Decision rule
keyIdea.text: Use ScriptableObjects for shared, persistent templates; use MonoBehaviours for instance-specific, runtime state and logic.

content.html:
Module 08 › Chapter 8.2 › SO vs MB
ScriptableObject

Asset-focused

  • Stored in Project as an asset and persistent across play sessions.
  • Best for templates: enemy types, item definitions, weapon data.
  • Editable in Inspector and reusable by many components.
Benefit: single source of truth for designers.
MonoBehaviour

Component-focused

  • Tied to GameObjects and scenes; handles instance state and behavior.
  • Good for per-instance health, position, AI state, and runtime timers.
  • May reference ScriptableObjects to retrieve configuration values.
Pitfall: duplicating static config across many components increases maintenance cost.
Quick Rule
If the value is shared and stable, make it an asset; if it changes per instance during play, keep it on a component.

screens.title: Editor Scripting Basics
screens.subtitle: How to extend the Inspector and build tools safely

narration.text: Editor scripting is the practice of writing code that extends the Unity Editor to improve workflows. All Editor scripts must be placed in a folder named Editor somewhere in your Assets folder. Code inside these folders is excluded from builds, which prevents editor-only utilities from inflating game size. Two common extension points are custom inspectors and Editor Windows. To make a custom inspector, create a class that inherits from Editor and decorate it with the CustomEditor attribute pointing at the target type. Override OnInspectorGUI and use EditorGUILayout or EditorGUI to draw fields, buttons, and validation messages. For Editor Windows, inherit from EditorWindow, add a static method with the MenuItem attribute to show the window, and implement OnGUI to compose the UI. The Editor A P I provides functions to mark assets dirty after changes and to operate on serialized properties. Common pitfalls include using runtime-only APIs inside Editor scripts or forgetting the Editor folder placement, both of which can lead to build errors or missing functionality. Well-constructed Editor scripts make designers faster and reduce human error. Editor Scripting Basics means place editor scripts in an editor folder, use editor classes for inspectors and editorwindow for full tools, and avoid runtime apis in editor code.. In practical terms, how to extend the inspector and build tools safely. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Editor rules
keyIdea.text: Place editor scripts in an Editor folder, use Editor classes for inspectors and EditorWindow for full tools, and avoid runtime APIs in editor code.

content.html:
Module 08 › Chapter 8.2 › Editor Scripting
Key Rules
  • Place editor code in an Editor folder to exclude it from builds.
  • Custom inspectors inherit from Editor and use [CustomEditor(typeof(...))].
  • EditorWindows inherit from EditorWindow and use [MenuItem] to add menu entries.
Benefit: tailored UIs reduce data entry errors.
Warning: mixing runtime APIs in editor scripts can cause errors during build.
Small Example
// Custom inspector signature
[CustomEditor(typeof(ItemData))]
public class ItemDataEditor : Editor
{
    public override void OnInspectorGUI()
    {
        // Use EditorGUILayout to draw fields and buttons
    }
}
Editor scripting gives you access to property drawers, serialized object handling, and handy UI primitives to validate and manipulate assets safely within the Editor context.

screens.title: Custom Inspector for ScriptableObjects
screens.subtitle: Improve designers' workflow with targeted UI and actions

narration.text: Creating a custom inspector for a ScriptableObject gives designers tailored controls and quick actions that a generic inspector does not provide. The pattern is to write an Editor class with the CustomEditor attribute pointed at your ScriptableObject type, for example ItemData. Inside OnInspectorGUI you can draw fields with EditorGUILayout. PropertyField or custom controls, add a simulate button that calls a supported method on the asset, and color-code fields based on an enum value to make authoring faster. The sample ItemDataEditor demonstrates how to display a header, render most fields, and add a button that calls UseItem on the asset. Remember to mark the asset dirty using EditorUtility. SetDirty when you modify fields so Unity saves changes. A misconception to avoid is assuming custom inspectors automatically run in builds; they only execute in the Editor. Use custom inspectors to validate dependencies, warn about missing prefabs, and add small utilities that reduce manual steps for designers. Custom Inspector for ScriptableObjects means custom inspectors use editor and oninspectorgui to present validation, buttons, and visual feedback for designers editing assets.. In practical terms, improve designers' workflow with targeted ui and actions. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Inspector pattern
keyIdea.text: Custom inspectors use Editor and OnInspectorGUI to present validation, buttons, and visual feedback for designers editing assets.

content.html:
Module 08 › Chapter 8.2 › Custom Inspector
Excerpt
[CustomEditor(typeof(ItemData))]
public class ItemDataEditor : Editor
{
    public override void OnInspectorGUI()
    {
        ItemData itemData = (ItemData)target;
        EditorGUILayout.LabelField("Item Configuration", EditorStyles.boldLabel);
        itemData.itemName = EditorGUILayout.TextField("Item Name", itemData.itemName);
        if (GUILayout.Button("Simulate Use Item"))
        {
            itemData.UseItem();
        }
        if (GUI.changed) EditorUtility.SetDirty(itemData);
    }
}
Practical Tips
  • Use EditorGUILayout for consistent layout across editor themes.
  • Mark objects dirty after changes to ensure persistence.
  • Provide clear labels and small helper buttons for frequent tasks.
Pro Tip
Keep inspectors focused: if a tool grows complex, extract it into an Editor Window instead of cramming too many controls into the Inspector.

screens.title: Editor Window essentials
screens.subtitle: MenuItem, OnGUI, and when to build a window

narration.text: Editor Windows are standalone Editor tools that are useful for workflows that need multiple steps, visualization, or batch operations. To create one, inherit from EditorWindow and add a static method with the MenuItem attribute to make the window appear under the Unity menu. Implement OnGUI to render UI using EditorGUILayout and EditorGUI calls. Unlike an inspector, Editor Windows can operate on multiple assets, draw custom visualizations, and expose persistent window state. Use them for tasks like a dialogue node editor or a level builder that automates prefab placement. Keep EditorWindows responsive by avoiding heavy computations in OnGUI and using EditorApplication. update for long operations. Another important point: because these are editor-only classes, they must live in an Editor folder. A common error is forgetting the MenuItem attribute or using runtime-only APIs inside the editor context. Well-designed windows bundle multi-step processes into a single reproducible interface that boosts team productivity. Editor Window essentials means use editorwindow plus menuitem and ongui for standalone tools that orchestrate multi-step workflows and visualize data.. In practical terms, menuitem, ongui, and when to build a window. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.text: Use EditorWindow plus MenuItem and OnGUI for standalone tools that orchestrate multi-step workflows and visualize data.

content.html:
Module 08 › Chapter 8.2 › Editor Window
Window Sketch
Key pieces: a MenuItem method to open the window, persistent window state across focus changes, and an OnGUI method that draws the UI using EditorGUILayout. Use EditorWindow for tools that manage many assets or require custom layouts and interactions.
Use case: a Dialogue Editor or Level Builder that places prefabs and serializes results.
Minimal pattern
public class MyToolWindow : EditorWindow
{
    [MenuItem("Window/My Tool")]
    public static void ShowWindow() => GetWindow("My Tool");

    void OnGUI()
    {
        // Draw GUI with EditorGUILayout
    }
}
Design windows for repeatable tasks. Extract complex interactions into helper classes and keep OnGUI focused on drawing and responding to user input.

screens.title: Editor scripting lifecycle & best practices
screens.subtitle: Placement, persistence, and avoiding build issues

narration.text: Understanding the lifecycle and best practices of Editor scripting prevents common errors and keeps projects maintainable. Always place editor-only code inside an Editor folder so Unity excludes it from builds. Use SerializedObject and SerializedProperty when editing serialized fields to ensure Unity's undo and prefab systems work correctly. When you change assets programmatically in the Editor, call EditorUtility. SetDirty so changes persist. Avoid referencing runtime-only APIs that don’t exist in the editor assembly or relying on scene-only state inside editor tools. For reusable utilities, write generic helper classes and expose small, well-documented public methods that other tools can call. Keep inspectors concise; if an inspector starts to manage complex multi-step flows, migrate that functionality into an Editor Window. Finally, include simple validation and warnings in inspectors to catch missing references early. These practices reduce friction for designers and prevent build-time surprises caused by misplaced or unsafe editor code. Editor scripting lifecycle & best practices means put editor scripts in editor folders, use serialized properties, set assets dirty after edits, and split complex tools into editor windows.. In practical terms, placement, persistence, and avoiding build issues. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Best practice summary
keyIdea.text: Put editor scripts in Editor folders, use serialized properties, set assets dirty after edits, and split complex tools into Editor Windows.

content.html:
Module 08 › Chapter 8.2 › Lifecycle & Practices
Checklist for safe editor code
  • Place scripts in an Editor folder to keep them out of builds.
  • Use SerializedObject and SerializedProperty for undo and prefab support.
  • Call EditorUtility.SetDirty after programmatic changes to assets.
  • Keep long-running tasks out of OnGUI; use update callbacks when needed.
  • Split complex UI into Editor Windows for clarity and reuse.
Pro-tip: small validation reduces designer mistakes early.
Common error: forgetting Editor folder placement causes build-time issues.

screens.title: Activity: ItemData & Custom Inspector

Module 08 › Chapter 8.2 › ItemData Lab
Step-by-step
  1. Create ItemData : ScriptableObject with CreateAssetMenu.
  2. Add fields: itemName, description with TextArea, icon, value, itemType enum.
  3. Create an Editor folder and an ItemDataEditor class inheriting from Editor.
  4. Use EditorGUILayout to draw fields and add a simulate button that calls UseItem().
  5. Mark the asset dirty when GUI.changed so edits persist.
Starter code
 // ItemData (Assets)
[CreateAssetMenu(fileName = "NewItemData", menuName = "Game Data/Item Data")]
public class ItemData : ScriptableObject
{
    public string itemName = "New Item";
    [TextArea(3,5)] public string description = "A generic item.";
    public Sprite icon;
    public int value = 1;
    public ItemType itemType = ItemType.Consumable;

    public enum ItemType { Consumable, Equipment, QuestItem }
    public void UseItem() { Debug.Log($"Using {itemName}!"); }
}
Test
Create the asset in Project, assign an icon, change values, and click the simulate button to confirm the debug output. Observe color or layout changes for different item types in your custom inspector.

screens.title: Validate assets and editor tools
screens.subtitle: Quick checks to ensure correctness and durable tools

narration.text: Validation and testing are essential parts of shipping editor tools and ScriptableObjects that teams rely on. Start with simple inspector checks: warn when required references are null, display clear error messages for invalid ranges, and visually flag enum values with color coding to communicate intent. For EditorWindows, include sanity checks when loading multiple assets, and provide Undo support where relevant. When running automated checks, ensure assets created programmatically are marked dirty and serialized so they save correctly. During testing, simulate designer actions: create assets from the Assets > Create menu, change fields, and confirm that runtime consumers reflect the new values without recompiling. Validate that editor scripts are placed inside an Editor folder so they do not cause build errors or appear in builds. Finally, include small integration tests where a PlayerWeapon reads a WeaponData asset and performs the expected instantiation or debug output. These steps catch common mistakes early and build confidence that tools behave predictably across the team. Validate assets and editor tools means add inspector warnings, null checks, undo support, and ensure editor code is correctly scoped to avoid build-time failures.. In practical terms, quick checks to ensure correctness and durable tools. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.text: Add inspector warnings, null checks, Undo support, and ensure Editor code is correctly scoped to avoid build-time failures.

Quick validation checklist

screens.title: Key Concepts — Part 1
screens.subtitle: What to remember from ScriptableObjects and Editor scripting

narration.text: Let's summarize the core concepts you need to remember. First, a ScriptableObject is a Unity class used to create persistent data assets; use it for configuration and shared templates, not ephemeral runtime state. Second, the CreateAssetMenu attribute makes your ScriptableObject type discoverable under Assets > Create so designers can author assets without code changes. Third, Editor scripting enables custom inspectors and Editor Windows that remove manual steps and surface validation; these scripts must live in an Editor folder so they are excluded from builds. These three points capture the most impactful practices: centralize configuration in assets, make asset creation discoverable, and build editor tools that reduce friction for non-programmers. Keep these ideas in mind when designing data models and tooling for your project. Summary

narration.text: Finish with three final reminders. First, custom inspectors let you present validation, helper buttons, and color-coded controls so designers edit assets faster and with fewer mistakes. Second, EditorWindows are the right choice when workflows require multi-step tools, visualization, or working with multiple assets at once; use MenuItem and OnGUI to create these windows. Third, include simple validation and persistence practices: check for null references, validate numeric ranges, mark objects dirty after edits, and ensure editor scripts live in Editor folders. Together these practices create reliable, designer-friendly pipelines where data and tools are clear, testable, and efficient. As you build tools, keep the user in mind and prefer small, focused inspectors with a migration path to windows when interactions grow complex.
